# Executive Summary

The project analyzes two datasets related to diabetes. A  dataset from Mendeley with 260+ patient records, and a CDC dataset with state-level diabetes prevalence rates. The analysis includes descriptive statistics, visualizations, and bias checks. Key findings include patterns in clinical markers across diabetes classes and potential imbalances in the datasets.

Our primary audience includes meidcal students, health researches, and public health officials who work in diabetes research. The purpose of this project is to provide insights into diabetes and remove the data cleaning burden many of these officals will have to do. By delivering a clean, structured SQL databse, researchers can focus strictly on analysis and skip the tedius extraction. Our EDA showed a strong positive correlation between HbA1c levels and diabetic classification. 



# Source & Extraction


Source 1: Mendeley Multiclass Diabetes Dataset (CSV) - This dataset was generated by Mendeley Data and contains a collection of over 200 patient records where biological markers were measured to classify then into 3 groups, Non Diabetic, Pre-Diabetic, and Diabetic. The data was collected from the iraqi society to study the disease in the Medical City Hospital. The variables are Gender, AGE, Urea(blood urea nitrogen level), Cr(creatine level), HbA1c, Chol, TG(triglycerides), HDL(healthy choloesterol), LDL(unhealth choloesterol), VLDL(low dense lipoprotien cholesterol), BMI, and Class (the diabetes classification).
https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/jpp8bsjgrm/1 

Source 2: CDC Diabetes State Burden Toolkit API (REST API) - This dataset is provided by the CDC and contains state-level diabetes prevalence rates. It was to help state health departments quantify the impact of diabetes through prevalence, incidence, and complications. It was collected in 2020. We set a limit to retrieve only 500 records from the API call. The variables in the data set are year, location, long_text_indicator, stratification_group1, data_value, lower_confidence_limit, upper_confidence_limit.
https://data.cdc.gov/Diabetes-State-level-Data/Diabetes-State-Burden-Toolkit-Health-Burden/ircd-wk4g/about_data


```{python}
import json
import requests as rq
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import sqlite3

# --- Source 1: Mendeley Multiclass Diabetes Dataset (CSV file) ---
mendeley = pd.read_csv("Multiclass Diabetes Dataset.csv")
print(f"Rows: {len(mendeley)}, Columns: {len(mendeley.columns)}")
print(mendeley.dtypes)
mendeley.head()

# --- Source 2: CDC Diabetes State Burden Toolkit API (REST API) ---
# Set limit ot 500 so we can get meaningful sample, don't need to much
url = "https://data.cdc.gov/resource/ircd-wk4g.json?$limit=500"

response = rq.get(url)
raw = json.loads(response.content)
print(f"Type: {type(raw)}")
print(f"Number of records: {len(raw)}")
print(f"Keys in first record: {list(raw[0].keys())}")
print(json.dumps(raw[0], indent=4))

# Convert to DataFrame
cdc_df = pd.DataFrame(raw)
print(f"Rows: {len(cdc_df)}, Columns: {len(cdc_df.columns)}")
print(cdc_df.dtypes)
cdc_df.head()
```


# Transformation Processes

The CDC dataset required converting most of the strings to numeric values, like data_value, lower_confidence_limit, upper_confidence_limit, and year. We also dropped two system generated geopgraphic columns because they are useless in our analysis and carry no weight. We also filtered out missing data and removed rows with negative values which would affect data. Additionally we filtered it to only post 2000 to keep it more up to date. 

The mendeley datset stored gender and class as numeric codes which makes the data really hard to interpret, so we mapped the codes into strings, 0 becomes "no diabetes", 1 becomes "pre-diabetic", and 2 becomes "diabetic", for gender 0 becomes "female" and 1 becomes "male". This makes the data much more readable and easier to work with.

Merging wasn't done because both of the datasets don't share a common key, especially since the mendeley dataset has no location or year column in the data. So instead of merging them, they're stored in seperate tables in the SQLite db. 


```{python}

# CDC Transformations

# Drop system-generated geographic region columns 
cdc_df = cdc_df.drop(columns=[
    ':@computed_region_hjsp_umg2',
    ':@computed_region_skr5_azej'
], errors='ignore')

# Convert numeric columns from string 
cdc_df['data_value'] = pd.to_numeric(cdc_df['data_value'], errors='coerce')
cdc_df['lower_confidence_limit'] = pd.to_numeric(cdc_df['lower_confidence_limit'], errors='coerce')
cdc_df['upper_confidence_limit'] = pd.to_numeric(cdc_df['upper_confidence_limit'], errors='coerce')
cdc_df['year'] = pd.to_numeric(cdc_df['year'], errors='coerce')

# Select only relevant columns
cdc_df = cdc_df[[
    'year', 'location', 'long_text_indicator',
    'stratification_group1', 'data_value',
    'lower_confidence_limit', 'upper_confidence_limit'
]]

# Removed rows with missing data_value
cdc_df = cdc_df.dropna(subset=['data_value'])

# Removed negative values
cdc_df = cdc_df[cdc_df['data_value'] >= 0]

# Filter to post-2000 data only
cdc_df = cdc_df[cdc_df['year'] > 2000]

cdc_df = cdc_df.reset_index(drop=True)

print(cdc_df.shape)
cdc_df.head()
```

```{python}
# Mendeley Transformations

# Map numeric codes to readable labels
mendeley['Class'] = mendeley['Class'].map({0: 'No Diabetes', 1: 'Pre-Diabetic', 2: 'Diabetic'})
mendeley['Gender'] = mendeley['Gender'].map({0: 'Female', 1: 'Male'})

mendeley = mendeley.reset_index(drop=True)

print(mendeley.shape)
mendeley.head()
```

```{python}

mendeley_cols = set(mendeley.columns)
cdc_cols = set(cdc_df.columns)

print("Mendeley columns:", mendeley_cols)
print("CDC columns:", cdc_cols)
print("Shared columns:", mendeley_cols.intersection(cdc_cols))
print("No shared key columns — datasets will remain as separate tables.")
```

# Analysis & Evaluation

## Mendeley Variables

- AGE
- Gender
- HbA1c: Hemoglobin A1c percentage, average blood sugar level for past 3 months
- BMI: Body Mass Index
- Urea: Blood Urea Nitrogen level
- Cr: Creatinine levels
- Chol: Total Cholesterol
- TG: Triglycerides;
- HDL: High-Density Lipoprotein
- LDL: Low-Density Lipoprotein
- VLDL: Very Low-Density Lipoprotein
- Class: Diabetes classification (0 = No Diabetes, 1 = Pre-Diabetic, 2 = Diabetic)

## CDC Variables 

- year 
- location
- long_text_indicator: Type of diabetes indicator (e.g., "Diabetes Prevalence", "Diabetes Incidence")
- stratification_group1: Demographic stratification
- data_value: Prevalence or incidence rate (numeric)
- lower_confidence_limit: Lower bound of confidence interval for data_value
- upper_confidence_limit: Upper bound of confidence interval for data_value

HbA1c is the strongest marker for classifying diabetes, averaging 4.58 for non-diabetics, 6.01 for pre-diabetics, and 8.84 for diabetics. BMI also follows a similiar pattern, which seems to increase with diabetes classification. Additionally, it is important to note that the Mendeley dataset is biased towards gender, withh 79/128 diabetic cases being male and female toward non-diabetic with 58/96 cases.

# Data Product & Guide

The final data product is a SQLite database named diabetes_data.db. It contains two tables, patient_records and cdc_burden. To open the database, download DB Browser for SQLite through the internet, then open the databse file directly. 

## Table 1: patient_records
- Gender
- AGE
- Urea
- Cr
- HbA1c
- Chol
- TG
- HDL
- LDL
- VLDL
- BMI
- Class (No Diabetes, Pre-Diabetic, Diabetic)

## Table 2: cdc_burden
- year
- location
- long_text_indicator
- stratification_group1
- data_value
- lower_confidence_limit
- upper_confidence_limit

```{python}
# SQLite Database

conn = sqlite3.connect("diabetes_data.db")

# Load both cleaned datasets as tables
mendeley.to_sql("patient_records", conn, if_exists="replace", index=False)
cdc_df.to_sql("cdc_burden", conn, if_exists="replace", index=False)

# Verify tables exist
tables = pd.read_sql("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table'", conn)
print(tables)

# Verify row counts match
print(pd.read_sql("SELECT COUNT(*) as patient_rows FROM patient_records", conn))
print(pd.read_sql("SELECT COUNT(*) as cdc_rows FROM cdc_burden", conn))

# patient_records table preview
print(pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM patient_records LIMIT 5", conn))

# cdc_prevalence table preview
print(pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM cdc_burden LIMIT 5", conn))

# Example queries
# Average A1c levels by Diabetes class
print(pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT Class, ROUND(AVG(HbA1c), 2) as avg_HbA1c, COUNT(*) as count
    FROM patient_records
    GROUP BY Class
    ORDER BY avg_HbA1c
""", conn))

# CDC Prevalence by year (averages)
print(pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT year, ROUND(AVG(data_value), 2) as avg_prevalence, COUNT(*) as records
    FROM cdc_burden
    GROUP BY year
    ORDER BY year
""", conn))

conn.close()
```
